stories.headline: Leavitt says Trump is defying midterm headwinds as he barnstorms country
stories.note: Karoline Leavitt says Trump is barnstorming battleground states and pushing his low-turnout voters to show up this time.
body: Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, speaking with Fox News Digital in her home state of New Hampshire, said President Trump is taking a tough midterm map head-on as Republicans work to hold their narrow House and Senate majorities.

Leavitt acknowledged the party in power usually loses seats in a midterm, and the article notes Republicans are also dealing with inflation, high gas prices and Trump's sagging approval numbers. But she said that history isn't slowing Trump down, pointing to recent stops in North Carolina and South Carolina and another trip to Michigan this weekend.

A big part of the pitch is turnout. Leavitt said Trump is telling MAGA voters plainly that he knows they tend to skip midterms, but that he needs them to vote this time. "The president is defiant, and he always is optimistic," she said.

On the other side, DNC Chair Ken Martin has claimed Republicans are "running scared" and spending heavily in deep-red areas. Leavitt countered that the race is a contrast between Republicans focused on tax cuts and border security and what she called some of the most radical Democratic candidates ever, and she pointed to a large GOP cash advantage.

Why it matters: Midterms usually come down to who shows up. With Trump personally campaigning and a money edge behind them, Republicans are betting they can turn out their base and beat the historical odds.

stories.headline: Obama prepares to rally with Michigan Dem who once delivered scathing verdict on his presidency
stories.note: Obama is campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, who once wrote that Obama 'was not the right choice,' while El-Sayed's support among Black voters looks shaky.
body: Former President Barack Obama is holding a Saturday rally for Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, after endorsing him in an ad that started running Oct. 12. The event also features Democratic governor nominee Jocelyn Benson.

The endorsement has revived attention on a 2012 Huffington Post essay in which El-Sayed criticized Obama over war, civil liberties and record deportations. In it he wrote that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one." El-Sayed has since softened those criticisms.

Republicans argue the campaign is leaning on Obama because El-Sayed is weak with Black voters, a key Democratic group in Michigan. He narrowly beat Rep. Haley Stevens in the primary while polls showed her doing better with Black Democrats, and a late-September Fox News Digital poll found just 77% of Black voters backing him, well below the usual Democratic level.

Fox News Digital talked with more than a dozen Black voters in Detroit and found many undecided voters unmoved by Obama's backing, with some calling El-Sayed's change of tune a flip-flop. Supporters such as Detroit government affairs professional Kandia Milton said the concerns are overblown and that Detroiters know El-Sayed well.
Why it matters: Michigan could decide Senate control. If Democrats can't fully energize Black voters there, that opens a real path for Republicans.

stories.headline: Omar’s deleted tweet could give clue on alleged marriage to her brother
stories.note: A resurfaced, deleted Omar post adds to the questions in the federal probe into her identity and immigration records.
body: A 2013 post by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., that was deleted in 2019 has resurfaced. In it, she wished a happy Father's Day to her father using the name "Nur Said," while records such as a 2020 Congressional Black Caucus memorial call him "Nur Omar Mohamed." The name is similar to that of her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

The post drew new attention after federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home on Oct. 12 as part of a criminal investigation into possible false statements on immigration and naturalization paperwork. Court papers tied to the search warrant refer to her as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, aka Ilhan Abdullahi Omar," and two people familiar with the probe told Fox News Digital that may be her legal name.

Omar denies wrongdoing, calls the investigation a political attack, and her office has repeatedly rejected claims that Elmi is her brother as a conspiracy theory. A statement circulated online and attributed to her spokesperson said "Nur Said" was her father's childhood nickname. Omar told Fox News Digital her real name is Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. The article also notes that similar Somali names alone don't prove a family relationship.

A former Minnesota federal immigration judge said that if investigators show Omar knowingly used a false name on federal forms, it could fall under the federal false statements law, depending on the documents and evidence of intent. The Justice Department did not comment.
Why it matters: Every new detail keeps the federal probe, and Omar's past, in the headlines, putting Democrats on defense over one of their most prominent progressives.

stories.headline: Second Amendment fight moves beyond guns with Supreme Court poised for big ruling
stories.note: Courts just struck down limits on switchblades and body armor, and gun-rights groups are hopeful ahead of a Supreme Court case on AR-15 bans.
body: Two court rulings on Wednesday widened Second Amendment protections. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals struck down a federal law restricting interstate commerce in switchblade knives, and a federal judge in western New York threw out the state's limits on civilians buying body armor. Both courts said those items count as protected "arms."

Both decisions applied the Supreme Court's Heller and Bruen rulings. Once the courts found the items were covered by the Second Amendment's text, the governments had to show a matching historical tradition of regulation, and in both cases they couldn't.

Gun-rights advocates say the reasoning sets up a bigger fight: Viramontes v. Cook County, where the Supreme Court will hear arguments on whether AR-15-style rifles are protected. The Seventh Circuit upheld Cook County's ban by comparing those rifles to machine guns, which Second Amendment attorney George Lyon called "just totally wrong."

The NRA's Justin Davis said courts are now sorting out what counts as an arm, from suppressors and magazines to stun guns and pepper spray. National Association for Gun Rights President Dudley Brown said a ruling against AR-15 bans could shape challenges to many of those restrictions.
Why it matters: A win in Viramontes would be a major victory for gun owners and a blow to Democratic-led assault weapons bans across the country.

stories.headline: Trump's war on drug cartels could gain powerful new ally after pivotal election
stories.note: Brazil could join Trump's anti-cartel coalition if conservative Flávio Bolsonaro wins today's runoff against Lula.
body: Brazil may join the U.S.-led anti-cartel coalition, known as the Shield of the Americas, if conservative Flávio Bolsonaro wins the country's Oct. 25 presidential runoff, his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

The coalition expands security cooperation across the Western Hemisphere, including intelligence sharing, military coordination and going after cartel money. It builds on the Trump administration's February 2025 move to label eight criminal groups, including Tren de Aragua, MS-13 and the Sinaloa Cartel, as terrorist organizations. Argentina, El Salvador and Peru take part, and the State Department lists others such as Ecuador, Panama, Paraguay and Chile.

Brazil hasn't joined under left-wing President Lula da Silva. Flávio Bolsonaro, who led Lula in the first round, has promised closer security ties with the U.S. "The main thing that we need to do is fight the cartels," Eduardo Bolsonaro said.

Adding Brazil would give the coalition a bigger footprint in South America, where gangs such as Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho dominate much of the drug trade. U.S. officials link cartels to fentanyl trafficking, and Sen. Tom Cotton has blamed cartel-linked overdoses for hundreds of thousands of American deaths.
Why it matters: A Bolsonaro win would hand Trump a major new partner in the hemisphere and strengthen his hardline push against the cartels.

stories.headline: Socialism's growing appeal meets an awkward reality check on college campus
stories.note: Michigan students who like socialism couldn't agree on what it means, and some admitted it would be less popular if people understood it.
body: A recent Fox News poll found 48% of Americans ages 18 to 34 view socialism favorably, compared with 32% of all Americans. Fox News Digital asked more than a dozen University of Michigan students to define it and got answers ranging from a bigger safety net to government or worker ownership of industry.

Some students described socialism as government paying for housing, health care and food. Others gave something closer to the textbook definition, government or collective control of major parts of the economy. At least a dozen students declined to be filmed because they said they didn't know enough to answer.

Several admitted their peers are confused. "If the definition was more widely known, people would support it less honestly," a student named Ahnika said. Others said people mix up socialism and communism, or use the word just as shorthand for good or bad.

The issue is live in Michigan's Senate race, where Republicans are tying Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed to socialism, a label he rejects despite past ties to the Democratic Socialists of America. Vice President JD Vance has warned that socialism becomes the alternative if people stop believing the American dream is within reach.
Why it matters: Socialism's popularity with young voters looks thin once you ask what it actually means, which strengthens the GOP case against DSA-linked Democrats in key races.
